module.subdomains.checks: Lists the subdomains known from certificate transparency logs (crt.sh, Cert Spotter as a fallback) and checks which ones still resolve.
module.subdomains.fix:
Compare the list of subdomains with your inventory (DNS host console, application list): every name must have a known owner and purpose.
For each name that is no longer used (old site, test, finished migration): delete its DNS record (A, AAAA or CNAME), shut down the server behind it and revoke its certificate if it is still valid.
For each name that resolves but must not be public (staging, administration, internal tools): restrict access (VPN, allow-list of addresses, strong authentication) or serve it only through an internal DNS.
Names show up here because they had a public certificate, and that publication is permanent: for future internal names, use an internal certificate authority, or a wildcard certificate (`*.example.com`) that does not list each name; then protect its private key carefully.
Check that every CNAME points to a target that still exists and belongs to you (subdomain takeover modules).
Run this scan again after every major release and at least once a quarter, to spot early a name you did not decide to publish.
module.subdomains.fix_snippet:
# Bash
while read -r name; do
  echo "$name $(dig +short "$name" | tr '\n' ' ')"
done < subdomains.txt

# PowerShell
Get-Content subdomains.txt | ForEach-Object { Resolve-DnsName $_ -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue | Select-Object Name, Type, IPAddress, NameHost }
module.subdomains.title: Subdomains
module.subdomains.why: Every subdomain is attack surface: test environments, old applications or forgotten services are often less protected than the main site.
